title: Black South Side nightclubs and their freedom of spirit
summary: Freeman describes going to black clubs solely for the music and the free spirit of the dancers despite their hardship.

story.theme_name: Gangsters, bootleggers and rough clubs of Prohibition
story.community_name: Gangsters, bootleggers and the Prohibition-era clubs

blocks.x: Here we were in black nightclubs where white people didn't go, and usually when a white man was out in a black nightclub in those early days, he was there to get a woman, I suppose or to get some booze, but we were there solely for the music. But not only did I witness something --
We were just talking about when
you were down on the South Side and what life, what you all saw there and the life that you saw.

Yes, well, as I say to repeat, because we had to change the tape, I saw this freedom of spirit that we whites didn't have. Now, of course, it's an easy thing for me to say that because these people were having a difficult time getting hold of money and they weren't given -- they weren't allowed any of the privileges and life could have been difficult for them but when they were out in the night life, out in a nightclub dancing, they just appeared to be so free in spirit and so happy.

Now, there again, the word happy, you know, it's a difficult word, because a lot -- many, many years ago when the whites, the majority of whites who did not understand that black man to say nothing of today, they could easily say, oh, they are all so happy and always smiling. Well, that's a cruel, stupid view to take. I don't mean that view, I only mean that they were free of spirit. They were not brainwashed by many things that we whites were taught to believe that aren't true of life.
